+# Teleport Level 5 job runner challenge
+This document discusses the proposed implementation of a simple job runner backend server and controlling CLI tool for
+the Teleport Level 5 challenge. The systems is designed to showcase my abilities as an engineer and my coding and
+development style. Other than acting as a replacement for simple Google searches for some specifics, and whatever
+auto-completion is provided by Jetbrains Goland 2025 (my IDE of choice), no AI has been used in this project.
+
+This is intended to be a living document. While the majority of the design is done before coding starts, it is
+inevitable that some details will change or some features be expanded upon as implementation progresses.
+
+## High Level Description
+This is a job runner service which allows authenticated users to run, stop, and inspect jobs running on a server. The
+server environment where the jobs will be run is a simple Linux server, with the only hard requirements being that it
+support cgroups v2 and uses systemd. The server administrator will need to create certificates for each user that is
+authorized to run jobs on the server, and client-server authentication will be done using mutual TLS, which in
+particular, will only support TLS 1.3.
+
+The server will expose a gRPC API for clients to interact with, and a simple CLI tool that uses those APIs will be
+provided. The minimal set of operations that the server will support are:
+- Start a job
+- Stop a job
+- Get the status of a job
+- List all running jobs
+- Stream the logs of a job
+- List all available jobs
+
+Both the server and the CLI tool will be implemented in Go, using only the standard library and a few well-known and
+widely used third-party libraries. No specific Go version is required but all development and testing was done using Go
+1.25 on an Ubuntu 24.04 LTS server. For certificate setup and creation, OpenSSL 3.0 or higher is required. A trivial
+improvement to the system would be to create a simple Go program that does this work, but the required OpenSSL is almost
+ubiquitous.
+
+### Nomenclature
+- Host: the backend hardware that runs the application and all jobs. Linux-based.
+- Library: the Go component that contains the logic for running and managing jobs.
+- Server: the job runner application that responds to gRPC requests and manages jobs using the library.
+- Client: the CLI tool that users will use to interact with the server.
+- Job: a process that is started by the server on behalf of a user using the client.
+- User: an individual who is authorized to use the system, using a unique certificate for authentication.
+- Job ID: a unique identifier for a job, assigned by the server when the job is started.
+
+## Deliverable Components
+The project will consist of several deliverable components:
+1. **Library**: A Go package that provides the core functionality for managing jobs, including starting, stopping and
+   monitoring jobs. Typically, this would not be a deliverable, but the task requirement mandate it so it will be provided.
+2. **Server**: A Go application that implements the gRPC server, handles client requests, and uses the library to manage
+   jobs. This will authenticate clients using mutual TLS (mTLS).
+3. **Client**: A Go application that provides a CLI for users to interact with the server, allowing them to start, stop,
+   and monitor jobs. This will also use mTLS for authentication.
+4. **Documentation**: Comprehensive documentation covering setup, usage, and design decisions.
+5. **Tests**: Unit and integration tests for the library, server, and client components.
+6. **Source Code**: All source code will be provided in a public [GitHub repository](https://github.com/jkj/telechallenge).
+
+## Personnel
+This project will be designed and implemented by Kean Johnston and reviewed by any personnel at Teleport that they deem
+necessary. No other personnel, real or virtual, will be involved in the design or implementation of the project.
+
+## Copyright
+All code in this project is in the public domain and the author asserts no copyright claims over it.
+
+## Timeline
+The project has been allocated 2 weeks for completion, beginning on August 26 2025 and ending on September 9 2025.
+The project will be deemed "accepted" by Teleport when they accept the final pull request in the GitHub repository.
+A proposed timeline is as follows:
+- **Day 1-2**: Document design and architecture, set up project structure and repository. Get all required collaborators
+  and reviewers on board in GitHub.
+- **Day 3**: Set up certificate generation and server configuration documentation and create scripts to automate the
+  process. Generate test certificates for development and testing. Address any design review issues.
+- **Day 4-6**: Implement the library component, including job management logic and interfaces.
+- **Day 7**: Implement all library tests and ensure appropriate test coverage.
+- **Day 8-9**: Implement the server component and tests.
+- **Day 10**: Implement the client component and tests.
+- **Day 11**: Finalize documentation, end-to-end tests, and prepare for delivery.
+- **Day 12-13**: Buffer day for any unforeseen issues or delays.
+
+# Hardware and Software Requirements
+The host can run on any hardware that supports a Linux operating system with cgroups v2 and `systemd`. This covers most
+modern Linux distributions including Ubuntu, Debian, Fedora, Arch and their derivatives, such as Mint. The reason for
+this is simple. `systemd` provides a simple and reliable way to manage cgroups, which are essential for resource
+management and isolation of jobs. It is completely possible to implement this without `systemd` and manually control
+cgroups, but that would increase the complexity of this project for very little value (such manual management involves
+creating the hierarchy and then manually writing various parameters to files in `/sys/fs/cgroup`, which has permission
+and ownership implications). `systemd` provides `systemd-run` for exactly this type of program, and using it
+addresses a number of edge cases that the requirements call out, such as correctly handling orphaned processes when the
+server crashes or is killed.
+
+*Note*: `systemd` is not required to run the server itself, only to manage the jobs that it spawns. The server can be
+run under any init system or even without one, as long as the host OS supports cgroups v2 and `systemd` is installed.
+
+*Note*: A future improvement would be to add support for non-`systemd` systems by manually managing cgroups, but this is not
+a requirement for this challenge, just that resource limits be enforced. Moving to a non-`systemd` model but using process
+groups and manually writing to cgroups control files, is easy, but not trivial. If the requirement to manage resources
+per job was lifted then this could trivially be portable enough to run on MacOS as well.
+
+The client has no specific requirements except for the ability to communicate with the server. Any host that Go can
+compile binaries for will be sufficient to run the client. The server administrator must have access to `openssl`
+version 3 or later to use the certificate creation scripts provided in this repository and discussed below.
+
+# Library Design
+The library is where the core business logic of the system is implemented. It deals with the actual starting, stopping,
+and monitoring of jobs. It is the meat of the server which is a relatively thin gRPC layer on top of it. Central to
+the library is the definition of a `Job`, which contains all of the static information about a job, a `JobID` which
+represents an a job that is actually currently running, and a `Manager` which is responsible for managing jobs.

+A `Job` is a struct which contains all the configurable fields relating to a job. The server manager will maintain a list
+of jobs that are available to be run, and a user can only start a job that is in this list. The fields are:
+
+```go
+package job
+
+type Role string
+const (
+    UserRole  Role = "user"
+    AdminRole Role = "admin"
+)
+
+type Job struct {
+    Name        string   `json:"name"`               // The name used for start / stop / status
+    Description string   `json:"desc"`               // A brief description
+    Role        Role     `json:"role,omitempty"`     // The role required, if any
+    Command     []string `json:"cmd"`                // The command, with arguments
+    Env         []string `json:"env,omitempty"`      // Environment variables
+    Dir         string   `json:"dir,omitempty"`      // The working directory or null for default
+    User        string   `json:"user,omitempty"`     // The user to run as or null for default
+    Group       string   `json:"group,omitempty"`    // The group to run as or null for default
+    Timeout     string   `json:"timeout,omitempty"`  // Timeout (1m, 1h, 30s etc) or empty for none
+    Memory      string   `json:"memory,omitempty"`   // Memory limit for the job, e.g. "512M", "2G", "" for none
+    CPU         string   `json:"cpu,omitempty"`      // CPU limit as percentage of 1 CPU (e.g. "50%", "200%"), "" for none
+    ExtraSD     []string `json:"extra_sd,omitempty"` // Extra systemd-run options
+}
+```
+
+The `Role` field is used to restrict access to certain jobs. A user must have the appropriate role to start a job. They are:
+- `user`: the default role, which all users have.
+- `admin`: an administrative role, which allows access to all jobs.
+
+The `Command` field is a slice of strings, where the first element is the command to run, and the subsequent elements
+are the arguments to the command. **Important**: the command and arguments are not interpreted by a shell, so shell
+features such as globbing, piping, redirection, and environment variable expansion will not work. If such features are
+required, the command must be run through a shell, e.g. `{"/bin/bash", "-c", "echo $HOME > output.txt"}`. In case the
+reader is not aware, it is the shell that expands things like `*` in `rm -f *.bak`, not the command itself, so use a
+shell if the job requires such features..
+
+## `JobID` Definition
+A `JobID` is a numeric identifier that represents a job that is currently running. It is a simple integer but it is
+given a distinct type to facilitate methods on it. A `JobID` is created when a job is started, and is used to refer to
+the job in subsequent operations such as stopping the job or getting its status. Users can make no assumptions about the
+value of a `JobID` other than that it is unique for the lifetime of the server. When the server is restarted, `JobID`s
+may be reused. Although this is in reality an ever-increasing integer, the caller can not assume this, and the server is
+free to change the implementation, including the type. Treat it as an opaque handle.
+
+```go
+package job
+
+type JobID uint64
+```
+
+## `Manager` Definition
+The `Manager` is the core of the library. It contains the configuration and defaults for the server and the list of running
+jobs. It also contains the required methods to manage jobs.
+
+```go
+package job
+
+// Type to hold configurable defaults for the manager.
+type Config struct {
+    Dir   string `json:"working_dir,omitempty"` // The default working directory for jobs
+    User  string `json:"user,omitempty"`        // The default user to run jobs as
+    Group string `json:"group,omitempty"`       // The default group to run jobs as
+    Certs string `json:"certs,omitempty"`       // The directory where job logs are stored
+    Port  string `json:"port,omitempty"`        // The port the server listens on or empty for 5871
+    Bind  string `json:"bind,omitempty"`        // The address the server binds to or empty for all
+}
+
+type Manager struct {
+    // Configuration fields populated from config.json
+    Jobs         map[string]Job   `json:"jobs"`     // The list of available jobs, keyed by name
+    Users        map[string]User  `json:"users"`    // The list of authorized users, keyed by unique email
+    Defaults     Config           `json:"defaults"` // The configurable defaults
+    DefaultDir   string           `json:"pwd"`      // The default working directory for jobs
+    DefaultUser  string           `json:"user"`     // The default user to run jobs as
+    DefaultGroup string           `json:"group"`    // The default group to run jobs as
+    CertDir      string           `json:"certs"`    // The directory where job logs are stored
+    
+    // Internal fields representing the state of the manager
+    nextJobID    atomic.Uint64       // The next JobID to assign
+    mu           sync.Mutex          // Mutex to protect access to Running
+    running      map[JobID]*Running  // The list of running jobs, keyed by JobID
+}
+
+type Running struct {
+    Job       *Job        // The job that is running
+    JobID     JobID       // The JobID assigned to this job
+    Who       *User       // The user who started the job, indexes Manager.Users.
+    StartTime time.Time   // The time the job was started
+    StdOut    *JobLog     // The stdout log
+    StdErr    *JobLog     // The stderr log
+}
+```
+
+### The `User` Definition
+A `User` represents an authorized user of the system. Each user has a unique email address, a role, and paths to their
+certificate and key files. The email address is used as the unique identifier for the user, and the role determines what
+jobs they are allowed to run. This would be the logical place to incrementally add value and features to the system,
+possibly defining things like per-user resource limits, job quotas, and so on.
+
+Please note that the user's email, which comes from the certificate's `SAN` field, is used as the unique identifier for
+the user and is not stored in the user structure itself, as it is the key used in the containing manager's `Users` map.
+
+```go
+package job
+
+type User struct {
+    Role  Role   `json:"role,omitempty"` // The role of the user
+    Cert  string `json:"cert"`           // The path to the user's certificate file
+    Key   string `json:"key"`            // The path to the user's key file
+}
+```
+
+When the server starts up and reads its configuration file, the `Cert` and `Key` fields will refer to the paths of those
+files. However, what is stored in memory is the actual *contents* of those files, as they are needed for mTLS
+authentication. The only reason that I don't just store the contents directly in the config file is that those files are
+managed by external tools and it is simpler to just point to them. If this was an actual product, I would make it such
+that there was an easy-to-use web front end for user management that would create the correct JSON configuration file.
+For this initial proof-of-concept version however, the config file will be manually managed. Referring to a file rather
+than embedding the contents is less error-prone and quicker to implement.

+A `Running` struct represents a job that is currently running. It contains a pointer the `Job`, the assigned `JobID`,
+who started the job and when, and pointers to the `JobLog` structs for the job's stdout and stderr logs. The main
+`Manager` struct contains a map of `Running` jobs, keyed by their `JobID`.

+A `Running` job will have the following method:
+- `Stop() error`: Stops the job. See the discussion below on process lifetime for details. Releases the resources associated
+  with the job.
+
+### The `JobLog` Definition
+The `JobLog` struct is a simple wrapper around a buffer that has a single writer and a fan-out of readers. It requires no
+locking as the writer is the only one that can modify the file, and the readers only read from it. The `JobLog` struct
+will have the following methods:
+- `Write(p []byte) (n int, err error)`: Writes data to the
+- `DumpFrom(start int64) ([]byte, error)`: Dumps the log from the specified byte offset.
+- `TailFrom(start int64) (<-chan []byte, func())`: Tails the log from the specified byte offset. The returned channel will
+  receive new output as it is written. The returned function must be called to stop the tailing (cancellation function).
comment.body: Fair point. It _should_ be a given, but we've seen fan-out mechanisms where all readers end up getting blocked by a single reader. Just a quick note of how the fan-out mechanism will handle a reader that is not ready to receive on the `<-chan []byte` would be great.

+    Dir         string   `json:"dir,omitempty"`      // The working directory or null for default
+    User        string   `json:"user,omitempty"`     // The user to run as or null for default
+    Group       string   `json:"group,omitempty"`    // The group to run as or null for default
+    Timeout     string   `json:"timeout,omitempty"`  // Timeout (1m, 1h, 30s etc) or empty for none
+    Memory      string   `json:"memory,omitempty"`   // Memory limit for the job, e.g. "512M", "2G", "" for none
+    CPU         string   `json:"cpu,omitempty"`      // CPU limit as percentage of 1 CPU (e.g. "50%", "200%"), "" for none
+    ExtraSD     []string `json:"extra_sd,omitempty"` // Extra systemd-run options
+}
+```
+
+The `Role` field is used to restrict access to certain jobs. A user must have the appropriate role to start a job. They are:
+- `user`: the default role, which all users have.
+- `admin`: an administrative role, which allows access to all jobs.
+
+The `Command` field is a slice of strings, where the first element is the command to run, and the subsequent elements
+are the arguments to the command. **Important**: the command and arguments are not interpreted by a shell, so shell
+features such as globbing, piping, redirection, and environment variable expansion will not work. If such features are
+required, the command must be run through a shell, e.g. `{"/bin/bash", "-c", "echo $HOME > output.txt"}`. In case the
+reader is not aware, it is the shell that expands things like `*` in `rm -f *.bak`, not the command itself, so use a
+shell if the job requires such features..
+
+## `JobID` Definition
+A `JobID` is a numeric identifier that represents a job that is currently running. It is a simple integer but it is
+given a distinct type to facilitate methods on it. A `JobID` is created when a job is started, and is used to refer to
+the job in subsequent operations such as stopping the job or getting its status. Users can make no assumptions about the
+value of a `JobID` other than that it is unique for the lifetime of the server. When the server is restarted, `JobID`s
+may be reused. Although this is in reality an ever-increasing integer, the caller can not assume this, and the server is
+free to change the implementation, including the type. Treat it as an opaque handle.
+
+```go
+package job
+
+type JobID uint64
+```
+
+## `Manager` Definition
+The `Manager` is the core of the library. It contains the configuration and defaults for the server and the list of running
+jobs. It also contains the required methods to manage jobs.
+
+```go
+package job
+
+// Type to hold configurable defaults for the manager.
+type Config struct {
+    Dir   string `json:"working_dir,omitempty"` // The default working directory for jobs
+    User  string `json:"user,omitempty"`        // The default user to run jobs as
+    Group string `json:"group,omitempty"`       // The default group to run jobs as
+    Certs string `json:"certs,omitempty"`       // The directory where job logs are stored
+    Port  string `json:"port,omitempty"`        // The port the server listens on or empty for 5871
+    Bind  string `json:"bind,omitempty"`        // The address the server binds to or empty for all
+}
+
+type Manager struct {
+    // Configuration fields populated from config.json
+    Jobs         map[string]Job   `json:"jobs"`     // The list of available jobs, keyed by name
+    Users        map[string]User  `json:"users"`    // The list of authorized users, keyed by unique email
+    Defaults     Config           `json:"defaults"` // The configurable defaults
+    DefaultDir   string           `json:"pwd"`      // The default working directory for jobs
+    DefaultUser  string           `json:"user"`     // The default user to run jobs as
+    DefaultGroup string           `json:"group"`    // The default group to run jobs as
+    CertDir      string           `json:"certs"`    // The directory where job logs are stored
+    
+    // Internal fields representing the state of the manager
+    nextJobID    atomic.Uint64       // The next JobID to assign
+    mu           sync.Mutex          // Mutex to protect access to Running
+    running      map[JobID]*Running  // The list of running jobs, keyed by JobID
+}
+
+type Running struct {
+    Job       *Job        // The job that is running
+    JobID     JobID       // The JobID assigned to this job
+    Who       *User       // The user who started the job, indexes Manager.Users.
+    StartTime time.Time   // The time the job was started
+    StdOut    *JobLog     // The stdout log
+    StdErr    *JobLog     // The stderr log
+}
+```
+
+### The `User` Definition
+A `User` represents an authorized user of the system. Each user has a unique email address, a role, and paths to their
+certificate and key files. The email address is used as the unique identifier for the user, and the role determines what
+jobs they are allowed to run. This would be the logical place to incrementally add value and features to the system,
+possibly defining things like per-user resource limits, job quotas, and so on.
+
+Please note that the user's email, which comes from the certificate's `SAN` field, is used as the unique identifier for
+the user and is not stored in the user structure itself, as it is the key used in the containing manager's `Users` map.
+
+```go
+package job
+
+type User struct {
+    Role  Role   `json:"role,omitempty"` // The role of the user
+    Cert  string `json:"cert"`           // The path to the user's certificate file
+    Key   string `json:"key"`            // The path to the user's key file
+}
+```
+
+When the server starts up and reads its configuration file, the `Cert` and `Key` fields will refer to the paths of those
+files. However, what is stored in memory is the actual *contents* of those files, as they are needed for mTLS
+authentication. The only reason that I don't just store the contents directly in the config file is that those files are
+managed by external tools and it is simpler to just point to them. If this was an actual product, I would make it such
+that there was an easy-to-use web front end for user management that would create the correct JSON configuration file.
+For this initial proof-of-concept version however, the config file will be manually managed. Referring to a file rather
+than embedding the contents is less error-prone and quicker to implement.
+
+### The `Running` Definition
+A `Running` struct represents a job that is currently running. It contains a pointer the `Job`, the assigned `JobID`,
+who started the job and when, and pointers to the `JobLog` structs for the job's stdout and stderr logs. The main
+`Manager` struct contains a map of `Running` jobs, keyed by their `JobID`.
+
+A `Running` job will have the following method:
+- `Stop() error`: Stops the job. See the discussion below on process lifetime for details. Releases the resources associated
+  with the job.
+
+### The `JobLog` Definition
+The `JobLog` struct is a simple wrapper around a buffer that has a single writer and a fan-out of readers. It requires no
+locking as the writer is the only one that can modify the file, and the readers only read from it. The `JobLog` struct
+will have the following methods:
+- `Write(p []byte) (n int, err error)`: Writes data to the
+- `DumpFrom(start int64) ([]byte, error)`: Dumps the log from the specified byte offset.
+- `TailFrom(start int64) (<-chan []byte, func())`: Tails the log from the specified byte offset. The returned channel will
+  receive new output as it is written. The returned function must be called to stop the tailing (cancellation function).
+- `Close() error`: Closes the log file.
+
+This type satisfies the `io.Writer` interface, so it can be used directly as the output for the command being run.
+
+### Job Status
+This system will not keep track of the exit status of jobs. When a job ends, it is removed from the list of running jobs
+and its resources are released. The user can inspect the server's logs to determine if it completed successfully. Any
+job that fails will eject a suitable message from the server, whose output can then be monitored for failure. I chose
+this approach to avoid having to store the exit status of jobs, which would require more complex state management and
+persistence.
+
+## Process Lifetime
+I have elected to use `systemd-run` to manage the lifetime of jobs. This is because `systemd` provides a robust and
+reliable way to manage processes and their associated cgroups. It addresses many of the requirements and edge cases and
+"fits in" with the system. The gRPC API will always provide a mechanism to stop a job, but the system administrator can
+also stop jobs using `systemctl` if needed. This makes jobs spawned by the job runner integrate better with host system
+and all the tools that the administrator is already familiar with.
+
+`systemd-run` also takes care of all the cgroup management, which is a non-trivial task if done manually. If we were to
+manage cgroups manually, we would have to create the cgroup hierarchy, set the appropriate limits, and ensure that the
+cgroups are cleaned up when the job ends. `systemd-run` handles all of this for us, which simplifies the implementation
+and reduces the potential for bugs.
+
+Using `systemd-run` and a simple exec also means we dont need to worry about setting the session ID, cleaning up orphaned
+processes, and other such details.
+
+## Other Job Considerations
+The `stdout` and `stderr` streams of each job are separated, and the log display and tailing commands only allow the user
+to stream / view one or the other. The client could set up two concurrent streams to get both, but this is left as an
+incremental system improvement for later.
+
+Logs are only stored in memory so there is no persistent data left on the system after a job ends. This is a deliberate
+design choice to keep the system simple and avoid having to manage log files. It reduces the attack surface of the system
+and ensures that sensitive data is not left on the system. The server administrator can always configure `systemd` to log
+the output of jobs to persistent storage if needed.
+
+## gRPC API Design
+The gRPC API is defined in the `proto/jobrunner.proto3` file. It defines the service and all the messages used in the API.
+The API is designed to be simple and easy to use. It provides the following methods:
+- `Start(JobName) returns (StartJobResponse)`: Starts a job. The request contains the name of the job to start. 
+  The response contains the assigned `JobID` if the job was started successfully or an error if it failed.
+- `Stop(JobID) returns (StopJobResponse)`: Stops a job. The request contains the `JobID` of the job to stop. Returns
+  true if the job existed and was stopped successfully, or an error otherwise.
+- `Status(JobID) returns (StatusResponse)`: Gets the status of the given `JobID`. Currently the only status is whether the
+  job is running or not, but this can be expanded in the future if needed. If the job is running but the owner is not the
+  caller, the response will be the same as if the job was not running.
+- `Running() returns (ListResponse)`: Lists all running jobs for the user. Returns the `JobID`, job name, when it was
+  started and by whom. If the user is an admin, all jobs are listed.
+- `Stream(JobID,which,start) returns (stream)`: Streams the logs of a job. `which` is `stdout` or `stderr`. Can `start` at
+  a specific byte offset, 0 for the begging of the file. The stream will continue to send new data as it is written to the
+  log, until the job ends or the client cancels the request. If the job is not running or the caller does not own the job,
+  no data will be returned and the stream will end immediately.
+- `Dump(JobID,which,start) returns (stream)`: Dump the logs of a job. `which` is `stdout` or `stderr`. Can `start` at
+  a specific byte offset, 0 for the begging of the file. Unlike `Stream` above, this simply dumps the extant contents and
+  ends when all the current data has been dumped.
+- `List() returns (JobList)`: Lists all available jobs that can be started given the caller's role. Returns an array of
+  `name:description` tuples.
+
+The API uses protocol buffers for message serialization, which is efficient and widely used.
+
+The client and server use mTLS for authentication. The server will use the client's certificate to identify the user and
+determine their role. The client will use the server's certificate to verify the server's identity.
+
+## Client Design
+The client is a simple CLI tool that uses the gRPC API to interact with the server. Running `jobcli --help` will display
+the following text, describing the available commands:
+
+```
+Usage: jobcli [options] <command> [<args>]
+Commands:
+  start <jobname>                 Start a job by name
+  stop <jobid>                    Stop a job by JobID
+  status <jobid>                  Get the status of a job by JobID
+  running (or ps)                 List all running jobs
+  stream <jobid> <which> [first]  Stream the logs of a job
+  dump <jobid> <which> [first]    Dump the logs of a job
+  list                            List all available jobs
+  
+Where <jobname> is one of the pre-defined jobs on the server as listed by
+'list', <jobid> is the numeric JobID assigned when the job was started with
+'start', <which> is either 'stdout' or 'stderr', and [first] is an optional
+byte offset to start streaming or dumping from (0 for beginning, the default).
+
+Options:
+  --server <host:port>            The server address (default "localhost:5871")
+  --cert <path>                   Path to the client's certificate file
+  --key <path>                    Path to the client's key file
+  --cacert <path>                 Path to the CA certificate file
+  --help                          Show this help message
+  
+'cert', 'key' and 'cacert' can also be set using the environment variables
+JOBCLI_CERT, JOBCLI_KEY and JOBCLI_CACERT respectively. They default to, in
+order, cert.pem, key.pem and ca-cert.crt, in $HOME/.jobcli.
+```
+
+Not much more needs to be said about the client, the above usage text is self-explanatory. The client will use mTLS to
+authenticate to the server, and will read the certificate, key, and CA certificate from the specified files.
+
+## Server Design
+The server is a gRPC server that implements the job runner service. It uses the library to manage jobs and handle client
+requests. The server will read its configuration from a JSON file, which will contain the list of available jobs, the
+list of authorized users, and the server's certificate and key files. An example configuration file is provided in the
+repository. The server will use mTLS to authenticate clients. It will use the client's certificate to identify the user
+and determine their role. The server will also use the server's certificate to verify its identity to clients.
+
+The definition of the `Manager` struct above contains all the JSON field names in the configuration file. The server
+will very explicitly *NOT* do any error checking of the config file contents other than to ensure that it is valid JSON.
+Rather than including error checking code that will only ever be used once at initialization, I will instead provide a
+simple Go program that reads a config file and checks it for validity, reporting any errors. This program can be run by
+the server administrator to validate the config file before starting the server. I will call this `jobcfgcheck`. A
+trivial startup sequence for the server would be: `jobcfgcheck && jobserver `.
+
+The server accepts a single optional argument, which is the name of the config file. All non-error status output will be
+sent to `stdout`, and all error output will be sent to `stderr`. The server will run in the foreground and can be
+managed using `systemd` or any other process manager. The server output is the only place where job execution status
+will be reported. This will always be in the form: `[JobID] job 'name' started by '$user'`, `[JobID] job 'name' completed
+successfully`, or `[JobID] job 'name' failed: error message`. Each such message will be prefixed with a timestamp. The
+server will not disassociate from its controlling TTY (daemonize) or write any PID or log files at all.
+
+The server will listen on port 5871 by default, but this can be changed using the configuration file. Unless given a
+specific address in the config file it will bind to all interfaces. All processes spawned by the server will inherit its
+environment, except for `HOME`, which will be set to the working directory specified in the config file, or the
+current working directory if none is specified.
+
+If the server terminates, all running jobs will be terminated. If it is restarted, any jobs that were running when it
+terminated will be lost. This is a deliberate design choice to keep the system simple and avoid having to manage
+persistent state. The server administrator can always configure `systemd` to restart the server if it crashes. The
+server will handle `SIGINT` and `SIGTERM` signals to allow for graceful shutdown. When the server receives one of these
+signals, it will stop accepting new connections, wait for all running jobs to complete, and then exit.

@@ -0,0 +1,343 @@
+# Teleport Level 5 job runner challenge
+This document discusses the proposed implementation of a simple job runner and controlling CLI tool for the Teleport
+Level 5 challenge. The system is designed to showcase my abilities as an engineer and my coding and development style.
+Other than acting as a replacement for simple Google searches for some specifics, and whatever auto-completion is
+provided by Jetbrains Goland 2025 (my IDE of choice), no AI has been used in this project.
+
+This is intended to be a living document. While the majority of the design is done before coding starts, it is
+inevitable that some details will change or some features be expanded upon as implementation progresses.
+
+## High Level Description
+
+This is a job runner service which allows authenticated users to run, stop, and inspect jobs running on a server. The
+server environment where the jobs will be run is a simple Linux server, with the only hard requirements being that it
+support cgroups v2. The server administrator will need to create certificates for each user that is authorized to run
+jobs on the server, and client-server authentication will be done using mutual TLS, which in particular, will only
+support TLS 1.3.
+
+The server will expose a gRPC API for clients to interact with, and a simple CLI tool that uses those APIs will be
+provided. The minimal operations that the server will support are:
+- Start a job
+- Stop a job
+- Get the status of a job
+- Stream the logs of a job
+
+Both the server and the CLI tool will be implemented in Go, using only the standard library and a few well-known and
+widely used third-party libraries. No specific Go version is required but all development and testing was done using Go
+1.25 on an Ubuntu 24.04 LTS server. For certificate setup and creation, OpenSSL 3.0 or higher is required. A trivial
+improvement to the system would be to create a simple Go program that does this work, but the required OpenSSL is almost
+ubiquitous.
+
+### Nomenclature
+- Host: the backend hardware that runs the application and all jobs. Linux-based.
+- Library: the Go component that contains the logic for running and managing jobs.
+- Server: the job runner application that responds to gRPC requests and manages jobs using the library.
+- Client: the CLI tool that users will use to interact with the server.
+- Job: a process that is started by the server on behalf of a user using the client.
+- User: an individual who is authorized to use the system, using a unique certificate for authentication.
+- Job ID: a unique identifier for a job, assigned by the server when the job is started.
+
+## Deliverable Components
+The project will consist of several deliverable components:
+1. **Library**: A Go package that provides the core functionality for managing jobs, including starting, stopping and
+   monitoring jobs. Typically, this would not be a deliverable, but the task requirement mandates it so it will be provided.
+2. **Server**: A Go application that implements the gRPC server, handles client requests, and uses the library to manage
+   jobs. This will authenticate clients using mutual TLS (mTLS).
+3. **Client**: A Go application that provides a CLI for users to interact with the server, allowing them to start, stop,
+   and monitor jobs. This will also use mTLS for authentication.
+4. **Documentation**: Comprehensive documentation covering setup, usage, and design decisions.
+5. **Tests**: Unit and integration tests for the library, server, and client components.
+6. **Source Code**: All source code will be provided in a public [GitHub repository](https://github.com/jkj/telechallenge).
+
+## Personnel
+This project will be designed and implemented by Kean Johnston and reviewed by any personnel at Teleport that they deem
+necessary. No other personnel, real or virtual, will be involved in the design or implementation of the project.
+
+## Copyright
+All code in this project is in the public domain and the author asserts no copyright claims over it.
+
+## Timeline
+The project has been allocated 2 weeks for completion, beginning on August 26 2025 and ending on September 9 2025.
+The project will be deemed "accepted" by Teleport when they accept the final pull request in the GitHub repository.
+A proposed timeline is as follows:
+- **Day 1-3**: Document design and architecture, set up project structure and repository. Get all required collaborators
+  and reviewers on board in GitHub.
+- **Day 4**: Set up certificate generation and server configuration documentation and create scripts to automate the
+  process. Generate test certificates for development and testing. Address any design review issues.
+- **Day 5-8**: Implement the library component and tests, including job management logic and interfaces.
+- **Day 9**: Implement the server component and tests.
+- **Day 10**: Implement the client component and tests.
+- **Day 11**: Finalize documentation, end-to-end tests, and prepare for delivery.
+- **Day 12-13**: Buffer day for any unforeseen issues or delays.
+
+# Hardware and Software Requirements
+The host can run on any hardware that supports a Linux operating system with cgroups v2.
+
+The client has no specific requirements except for the ability to communicate with the server.
+
+# Library Design
+The library is where the core business logic of the system is implemented. It deals with the actual starting, stopping,
+and monitoring of jobs. This library will manage the lifecycle of jobs, including setting up cgroups, handling
+stdout/stderr logging, and enforcing resource limits. The `Manager` struct contains the configuration and state of the job
+runner, including the list of running and completed jobs. Running and completed jobs each have a unique `JobID` assigned.
+The `Jobs` map contains a list of all jobs, indexed by `JobID`.
+
+## Configurable Values
+To reduce the scope of the project the following constants are used to configure the server, which ideally would be
+configurable by the server administrator. My inclination would be to use a simple JSON config file as that is trivially
+parsed by Go and lends itself to easy editing by the administrator (or one day writing a small web front end to edit it).
+
+- Default working directory for jobs: `/tmp`
+- Default user to run jobs as: `nobody`
+- Default group to run jobs as: `nogroup`
+- Port the server listens on: `5871`
+- Memory limit per job: `1G`
+- CPU limit per job: `100%` of 1 CPU
+- Disk I/O limit per job: none
+
+These will all be stored in the file `tunable.go` in the library package.
+
+## The `Job` Type
+```go
+package job
+
+type Job struct {
+  command  []string   // The command, with arguments
+  pid      int        // The PID of the process, 0 if it has exited
+  user     string     // The user who launched the job (email), from their certificate
+  started  time.Time  // When the job was started
+  finished time.Time  // When the job finished, valid only if pid is 0
+  exitCode int        // The exit code of the job, valid only if pid is 0
+  stdout    *JobLog   // The stdout log
+  stderr    *JobLog   // The stderr log
+}
+```
+
+A `Job` is a struct which contains all the fields relating to a job, either running or complete. It also contains the
+`JobLog` structs for the job's stdout and stderr logs.
+
+The `command` field is a slice of strings, where the first element is the command to run, and the subsequent elements
+are the arguments to the command. **Important**: the command and arguments are not interpreted by a shell, so shell
+features such as globbing, piping, redirection, and environment variable expansion will not work. If such features are
+required, the command must be run through a shell, e.g. `{ "/bin/bash", "-c", "rm", "-f", "*.bak" }`.
+
+TODO: the CLI could easily add a `shell` option that automatically wraps its args in `/bin/bash -c`. Its not important
+enough to do now but it is a very easy convenience feature to add.
+
+### The `JobLog` Type
+`JobLog` (not shown here, please see `joblog.go`) is a simple chunked buffer that has a single writer and any number of
+readers. By "chunked" I mean that it stores the data in a slice of byte slices, each of which is a chunk of data. This
+allows for efficient appending and reading of data. The chunk size is hard-coded to 4K, which is probably reasonable for
+this implementation, but could easily be made a parameter. The log is stored entirely in memory.

+// protobufs specification for the Teleport Level 5 interview challenge.
+// A very simple API to start, stop, check and tail the logs of arbitrary
+// Linux processes on a server. It has been a while since I used RPCs so
+// this may not be optimal. Please tell me if I have done anything wrong!
+
+// To generate the code I used protoc 3.21.12, google.golang.org/grpc v1.75.0
+// google.golang.org/protobuf v1.36.6 and in the top level directory (the one
+// with go.mod) I executed: ./scripts/generate-rpc
+
+syntax = "proto3";
+
+package jobs.v1;
+
+option go_package = "github.com/jkj/telechallenge/gen/jobs/v1;jobsproto";
+
+// All errors via gRPC status, not as part of the command reply. That is, if
+// the gRPC call fails and returns an error, the response field is invalid.
+service JobService {
+  // Start a job given an argv-style list. argv[0] is the program path.
+  rpc Start(StartRequest) returns (RequestResponse);
+
+  // Query status text for a job_id.
+  rpc Status(JobID) returns (RequestResponse);
comment.body:
> What would the `string message` in the `RequestResponse` include for the status? Can you think of a less opaque API that conveys more details?

The only real information we have about a job is whether it was still running, had run to completion, or was stopped. There isnt really anything that can be done with that information except to stop a running job. I was operating under repeated instructions to keep things simple, and take shortcuts. This was one of them. I was planning on returning one of 3 strings:

`Job 123 still running`
`Job 123 stopped by user`
`Job 123 finished with exit code 0`

I can easily surface the information in the API. It did occur to me that there is one piece of information not exposed that would be useful - the time the job started. That could easily be returned in such a message, or it can be returned by the API as the response and let the front-end format the display of the status. So in essence, I would see the following being useful in a response reply:
1. The current status of the job. This could be an enum: RUNNING, STOPPED, EXITED.

+# Teleport Level 5 job runner challenge
+This document discusses the proposed implementation of a simple job runner and controlling CLI tool for the Teleport
+Level 5 challenge. The system is designed to showcase my abilities as an engineer and my coding and development style.
+Other than acting as a replacement for simple Google searches for some specifics, and whatever auto-completion is
+provided by Jetbrains Goland 2025 (my IDE of choice), no AI has been used in this project.
+
+This is intended to be a living document. While the majority of the design is done before coding starts, it is
+inevitable that some details will change or some features be expanded upon as implementation progresses.
+
+## High Level Description
+
+This is a job runner service which allows authenticated users to run, stop, and inspect jobs running on a server. The
+server environment where the jobs will be run is a simple Linux server, with the only hard requirements being that it
+support cgroups v2. The server administrator will need to create certificates for each user that is authorized to run
+jobs on the server, and client-server authentication will be done using mutual TLS, which in particular, will only
+support TLS 1.3.
+
+The server will expose a gRPC API for clients to interact with, and a simple CLI tool that uses those APIs will be
+provided. The minimal operations that the server will support are:
+- Start a job
+- Stop a job
+- Get the status of a job
+- Stream the logs of a job
+
+Both the server and the CLI tool will be implemented in Go, using only the standard library and a few well-known and
+widely used third-party libraries. No specific Go version is required but all development and testing was done using Go
+1.25 on an Ubuntu 24.04 LTS server. For certificate setup and creation, OpenSSL 3.0 or higher is required. A trivial
+improvement to the system would be to create a simple Go program that does this work, but the required OpenSSL is almost
+ubiquitous.
+
+### Nomenclature
+- Host: the backend hardware that runs the application and all jobs. Linux-based.
+- Library: the Go component that contains the logic for running and managing jobs.
+- Server: the job runner application that responds to gRPC requests and manages jobs using the library.
+- Client: the CLI tool that users will use to interact with the server.
+- Job: a process that is started by the server on behalf of a user using the client.
+- User: an individual who is authorized to use the system, using a unique certificate for authentication.
+- Job ID: a unique identifier for a job, assigned by the server when the job is started.
+
+## Deliverable Components
+The project will consist of several deliverable components:
+1. **Library**: A Go package that provides the core functionality for managing jobs, including starting, stopping and
+   monitoring jobs. Typically, this would not be a deliverable, but the task requirement mandates it so it will be provided.
+2. **Server**: A Go application that implements the gRPC server, handles client requests, and uses the library to manage
+   jobs. This will authenticate clients using mutual TLS (mTLS).
+3. **Client**: A Go application that provides a CLI for users to interact with the server, allowing them to start, stop,
+   and monitor jobs. This will also use mTLS for authentication.
+4. **Documentation**: Comprehensive documentation covering setup, usage, and design decisions.
+5. **Tests**: Unit and integration tests for the library, server, and client components.
+6. **Source Code**: All source code will be provided in a public [GitHub repository](https://github.com/jkj/telechallenge).
+
+## Personnel
+This project will be designed and implemented by Kean Johnston and reviewed by any personnel at Teleport that they deem
+necessary. No other personnel, real or virtual, will be involved in the design or implementation of the project.
+
+## Copyright
+All code in this project is in the public domain and the author asserts no copyright claims over it.
+
+## Timeline
+The project has been allocated 2 weeks for completion, beginning on August 26 2025 and ending on September 9 2025.
+The project will be deemed "accepted" by Teleport when they accept the final pull request in the GitHub repository.
+A proposed timeline is as follows:
+- **Day 1-3**: Document design and architecture, set up project structure and repository. Get all required collaborators
+  and reviewers on board in GitHub.
+- **Day 4**: Set up certificate generation and server configuration documentation and create scripts to automate the
+  process. Generate test certificates for development and testing. Address any design review issues.
+- **Day 5-8**: Implement the library component and tests, including job management logic and interfaces.
+- **Day 9**: Implement the server component and tests.
+- **Day 10**: Implement the client component and tests.
+- **Day 11**: Finalize documentation, end-to-end tests, and prepare for delivery.
+- **Day 12-13**: Buffer day for any unforeseen issues or delays.
+
+# Hardware and Software Requirements
+The host can run on any hardware that supports a Linux operating system with cgroups v2.
+
+The client has no specific requirements except for the ability to communicate with the server.
+
+# Library Design
+The library is where the core business logic of the system is implemented. It deals with the actual starting, stopping,
+and monitoring of jobs. This library will manage the lifecycle of jobs, including setting up cgroups, handling
+stdout/stderr logging, and enforcing resource limits. The `Manager` struct contains the configuration and state of the job
+runner, including the list of running and completed jobs. Running and completed jobs each have a unique `JobID` assigned.
+The `Jobs` map contains a list of all jobs, indexed by `JobID`.
+
+## Configurable Values
+To reduce the scope of the project the following constants are used to configure the server, which ideally would be
+configurable by the server administrator. My inclination would be to use a simple JSON config file as that is trivially
+parsed by Go and lends itself to easy editing by the administrator (or one day writing a small web front end to edit it).
+
+- Default working directory for jobs: `/tmp`
+- Default user to run jobs as: `nobody`
+- Default group to run jobs as: `nogroup`
+- Port the server listens on: `5871`
+- Memory limit per job: `1G`
+- CPU limit per job: `100%` of 1 CPU
+- Disk I/O limit per job: none
+
+These will all be stored in the file `tunable.go` in the library package.
+
+## The `Job` Type
+```go
+package job
+
+type Job struct {
+  command  []string   // The command, with arguments
+  pid      int        // The PID of the process, 0 if it has exited
+  user     string     // The user who launched the job (email), from their certificate
+  started  time.Time  // When the job was started
+  finished time.Time  // When the job finished, valid only if pid is 0
+  exitCode int        // The exit code of the job, valid only if pid is 0
+  stdout    *JobLog   // The stdout log
+  stderr    *JobLog   // The stderr log
+}
+```
+
+A `Job` is a struct which contains all the fields relating to a job, either running or complete. It also contains the
+`JobLog` structs for the job's stdout and stderr logs.
+
+The `command` field is a slice of strings, where the first element is the command to run, and the subsequent elements
+are the arguments to the command. **Important**: the command and arguments are not interpreted by a shell, so shell
+features such as globbing, piping, redirection, and environment variable expansion will not work. If such features are
+required, the command must be run through a shell, e.g. `{ "/bin/bash", "-c", "rm", "-f", "*.bak" }`.
+
+TODO: the CLI could easily add a `shell` option that automatically wraps its args in `/bin/bash -c`. Its not important
+enough to do now but it is a very easy convenience feature to add.
+
+### The `JobLog` Type
+`JobLog` (not shown here, please see `joblog.go`) is a simple chunked buffer that has a single writer and any number of
+readers. By "chunked" I mean that it stores the data in a slice of byte slices, each of which is a chunk of data. This
+allows for efficient appending and reading of data. The chunk size is hard-coded to 4K, which is probably reasonable for
+this implementation, but could easily be made a parameter. The log is stored entirely in memory.

+jobs on the server, and client-server authentication will be done using mutual TLS, which in particular, will only
+support TLS 1.3.
+
+The server will expose a gRPC API for clients to interact with, and a simple CLI tool that uses those APIs will be
+provided. The minimal operations that the server will support are:
+- Start a job
+- Stop a job
+- Get the status of a job
+- Stream the logs of a job
+
+Both the server and the CLI tool will be implemented in Go, using only the standard library and a few well-known and
+widely used third-party libraries. No specific Go version is required but all development and testing was done using Go
+1.25 on an Ubuntu 24.04 LTS server. For certificate setup and creation, OpenSSL 3.0 or higher is required. A trivial
+improvement to the system would be to create a simple Go program that does this work, but the required OpenSSL is almost
+ubiquitous.
+
+### Nomenclature
+- Host: the backend hardware that runs the application and all jobs. Linux-based.
+- Library: the Go component that contains the logic for running and managing jobs.
+- Server: the job runner application that responds to gRPC requests and manages jobs using the library.
+- Client: the CLI tool that users will use to interact with the server.
+- Job: a process that is started by the server on behalf of a user using the client.
+- User: an individual who is authorized to use the system, using a unique certificate for authentication.
+- Job ID: a unique identifier for a job, assigned by the server when the job is started.
+
+## Deliverable Components
+The project will consist of several deliverable components:
+1. **Library**: A Go package that provides the core functionality for managing jobs, including starting, stopping and
+   monitoring jobs. Typically, this would not be a deliverable, but the task requirement mandates it so it will be provided.
+2. **Server**: A Go application that implements the gRPC server, handles client requests, and uses the library to manage
+   jobs. This will authenticate clients using mutual TLS (mTLS).
+3. **Client**: A Go application that provides a CLI for users to interact with the server, allowing them to start, stop,
+   and monitor jobs. This will also use mTLS for authentication.
+4. **Documentation**: Comprehensive documentation covering setup, usage, and design decisions.
+5. **Tests**: Unit and integration tests for the library, server, and client components.
+6. **Source Code**: All source code will be provided in a public [GitHub repository](https://github.com/jkj/telechallenge).
+
+## Personnel
+This project will be designed and implemented by Kean Johnston and reviewed by any personnel at Teleport that they deem
+necessary. No other personnel, real or virtual, will be involved in the design or implementation of the project.

+All code in this project is in the public domain and the author asserts no copyright claims over it.

+The project has been allocated 2 weeks for completion, beginning on August 26 2025 and ending on September 9 2025.
+The project will be deemed "accepted" by Teleport when they accept the final pull request in the GitHub repository.
+A proposed timeline is as follows:
+- **Day 1-3**: Document design and architecture, set up project structure and repository. Get all required collaborators
+  and reviewers on board in GitHub.
+- **Day 4**: Set up certificate generation and server configuration documentation and create scripts to automate the
+  process. Generate test certificates for development and testing. Address any design review issues.
+- **Day 5-8**: Implement the library component and tests, including job management logic and interfaces.
+- **Day 9**: Implement the server component and tests.
+- **Day 10**: Implement the client component and tests.
+- **Day 11**: Finalize documentation, end-to-end tests, and prepare for delivery.
+- **Day 12-13**: Buffer day for any unforeseen issues or delays.
+
+# Hardware and Software Requirements
+The host can run on any hardware that supports a Linux operating system with cgroups v2.
+
+The client has no specific requirements except for the ability to communicate with the server.
+
+# Library Design
+The library is where the core business logic of the system is implemented. It deals with the actual starting, stopping,
+and monitoring of jobs. This library will manage the lifecycle of jobs, including setting up cgroups, handling
+stdout/stderr logging, and enforcing resource limits. The `Manager` struct contains the configuration and state of the job
+runner, including the list of running and completed jobs. Running and completed jobs each have a unique `JobID` assigned.
+The `Jobs` map contains a list of all jobs, indexed by `JobID`.
+
+## Configurable Values
+To reduce the scope of the project the following constants are used to configure the server, which ideally would be
+configurable by the server administrator. My inclination would be to use a simple JSON config file as that is trivially
+parsed by Go and lends itself to easy editing by the administrator (or one day writing a small web front end to edit it).
+
+- Default working directory for jobs: `/tmp`
+- Default user to run jobs as: `nobody`
+- Default group to run jobs as: `nogroup`
+- Port the server listens on: `5871`
+- Memory limit per job: `1G`
+- CPU limit per job: `100%` of 1 CPU
+- Disk I/O limit per job: none
+
+These will all be stored in the file `tunable.go` in the library package.
+
+## The `Job` Type
+```go
+package job
+
+type Job struct {
+  command  []string   // The command, with arguments
+  pid      int        // The PID of the process, 0 if it has exited
+  user     string     // The user who launched the job (email), from their certificate
+  started  time.Time  // When the job was started
+  finished time.Time  // When the job finished, valid only if pid is 0
+  exitCode int        // The exit code of the job, valid only if pid is 0
+  stdout    *JobLog   // The stdout log
+  stderr    *JobLog   // The stderr log
+}
+```
+
+A `Job` is a struct which contains all the fields relating to a job, either running or complete. It also contains the
+`JobLog` structs for the job's stdout and stderr logs.
+
+The `command` field is a slice of strings, where the first element is the command to run, and the subsequent elements
+are the arguments to the command. **Important**: the command and arguments are not interpreted by a shell, so shell
+features such as globbing, piping, redirection, and environment variable expansion will not work. If such features are
+required, the command must be run through a shell, e.g. `{ "/bin/bash", "-c", "rm", "-f", "*.bak" }`.
+
+TODO: the CLI could easily add a `shell` option that automatically wraps its args in `/bin/bash -c`. Its not important
+enough to do now but it is a very easy convenience feature to add.
+
+### The `JobLog` Type
+`JobLog` (not shown here, please see `joblog.go`) is a simple chunked buffer that has a single writer and any number of
+readers. By "chunked" I mean that it stores the data in a slice of byte slices, each of which is a chunk of data. This
+allows for efficient appending and reading of data. The chunk size is hard-coded to 4K, which is probably reasonable for
+this implementation, but could easily be made a parameter. The log is stored entirely in memory.
+
+Each `JobLog` is locked very briefly as new data is written to it. It will have a condition variable on which readers
+will wait, and that is broadcast to whenever new data is written. Each reader keeps track of its own position in the
+log, so that it can read from the log independently of other readers. This allows multiple clients to read from the log
+simultaneously, each at their own pace. Each reader holds the lock very briefly to take a snapshot of the chunk pointer
+and position. Reading from this pointer isn't locked because the chunk can only be appended to, not modified or deleted.
+
+`JobLog` satisfies the `io.Writer` interface. This means they can be used for the `Stdout` and `Stderr` fields of the
+`exec.Cmd` struct. This is how we feed the logs from the job process into the system.
+
+## The `JobID` Type
+A `JobID` is a numeric identifier that represents a job that is currently running. It is a simple integer, but it is
+given a distinct type to facilitate methods on it. A `JobID` is created when a job is started, and is used to refer to
+the job in subsequent operations such as stopping the job or getting its status. Users should make no assumptions about
+the value of a `JobID` other than that it is unique for the lifetime of the server. Treat it as an opaque handle.
+
+Please see the end of this document for comments about the current implementation.
+
+## The `Manager` Type
+In a more fleshed out version, this would contain the configuration options that are hard-coded for this challenge. See
+the above section on configurable values. It contains the list of jobs, indexed by `JobID`. There is a mutex to protect
+adding a new job and incrementing the next job ID (reading it is atomic but only the locked code needs to read it anyway
+so the point is moot).
+
+```go
+package job
+
+type JobID uint64
+
+type Manager struct {
+    jobs      map[JobID]Job  // The list of jobs, keyed by JobID
+    nextJobID JobID          // The next JobID to assign
+    mu        sync.Mutex     // Mutex to protect access to Jobs
+}
+```
+
+## The User Certificate
+A user is defined by their certificate, which will contain their email address and optionally the Linux user and group to
+use when running jobs. All three fields will be stored in the certificate's `subjectAltName` field. The email address will
+use `rfc822Name`, while the user and group will use custom URI entries of the form `uri:user:username` etc. For example:
+
+```
+subjectAltName=rfc822Name:kean@example.com,uri:user:kean,uri:group:staff
+```
+
+If no user (or group) is specified in SAN, the server will use the default user (`nobody`) and group (`nogroup`)
+specified in the `tunable.go` file. This ensures that jobs don't run as root (the server runs as root).
+
+Generation of a user certificate from a CSR should exclude any `subjectAltName` fields from the CSR.
+

+# Teleport Level 5 job runner challenge
+This document discusses the proposed implementation of a simple job runner backend server and controlling CLI tool for
+the Teleport Level 5 challenge. The systems is designed to showcase my abilities as an engineer and my coding and
+development style. Other than acting as a replacement for simple Google searches for some specifics, and whatever
+auto-completion is provided by Jetbrains Goland 2025 (my IDE of choice), no AI has been used in this project.
+
+This is intended to be a living document. While the majority of the design is done before coding starts, it is
+inevitable that some details will change or some features be expanded upon as implementation progresses.
+
+## High Level Description
+This is a job runner service which allows authenticated users to run, stop, and inspect jobs running on a server. The
+server environment where the jobs will be run is a simple Linux server, with the only hard requirements being that it
+support cgroups v2 and uses systemd. The server administrator will need to create certificates for each user that is
+authorized to run jobs on the server, and client-server authentication will be done using mutual TLS, which in
+particular, will only support TLS 1.3.
+
+The server will expose a gRPC API for clients to interact with, and a simple CLI tool that uses those APIs will be
+provided. The minimal set of operations that the server will support are:
+- Start a job
+- Stop a job
+- Get the status of a job
+- List all running jobs
+- Stream the logs of a job
+- List all available jobs
+
+Both the server and the CLI tool will be implemented in Go, using only the standard library and a few well-known and
+widely used third-party libraries. No specific Go version is required but all development and testing was done using Go
+1.25 on an Ubuntu 24.04 LTS server. For certificate setup and creation, OpenSSL 3.0 or higher is required. A trivial
+improvement to the system would be to create a simple Go program that does this work, but the required OpenSSL is almost
+ubiquitous.
+
+### Nomenclature
+- Host: the backend hardware that runs the application and all jobs. Linux-based.
+- Library: the Go component that contains the logic for running and managing jobs.
+- Server: the job runner application that responds to gRPC requests and manages jobs using the library.
+- Client: the CLI tool that users will use to interact with the server.
+- Job: a process that is started by the server on behalf of a user using the client.
+- User: an individual who is authorized to use the system, using a unique certificate for authentication.
+- Job ID: a unique identifier for a job, assigned by the server when the job is started.
+
+## Deliverable Components
+The project will consist of several deliverable components:
+1. **Library**: A Go package that provides the core functionality for managing jobs, including starting, stopping and
+   monitoring jobs. Typically, this would not be a deliverable, but the task requirement mandate it so it will be provided.
+2. **Server**: A Go application that implements the gRPC server, handles client requests, and uses the library to manage
+   jobs. This will authenticate clients using mutual TLS (mTLS).
+3. **Client**: A Go application that provides a CLI for users to interact with the server, allowing them to start, stop,
+   and monitor jobs. This will also use mTLS for authentication.
+4. **Documentation**: Comprehensive documentation covering setup, usage, and design decisions.
+5. **Tests**: Unit and integration tests for the library, server, and client components.
+6. **Source Code**: All source code will be provided in a public [GitHub repository](https://github.com/jkj/telechallenge).
+
+## Personnel
+This project will be designed and implemented by Kean Johnston and reviewed by any personnel at Teleport that they deem
+necessary. No other personnel, real or virtual, will be involved in the design or implementation of the project.
+
+## Copyright
+All code in this project is in the public domain and the author asserts no copyright claims over it.
+
+## Timeline
+The project has been allocated 2 weeks for completion, beginning on August 26 2025 and ending on September 9 2025.
+The project will be deemed "accepted" by Teleport when they accept the final pull request in the GitHub repository.
+A proposed timeline is as follows:
+- **Day 1-2**: Document design and architecture, set up project structure and repository. Get all required collaborators
+  and reviewers on board in GitHub.
+- **Day 3**: Set up certificate generation and server configuration documentation and create scripts to automate the
+  process. Generate test certificates for development and testing. Address any design review issues.
+- **Day 4-6**: Implement the library component, including job management logic and interfaces.
+- **Day 7**: Implement all library tests and ensure appropriate test coverage.
+- **Day 8-9**: Implement the server component and tests.
+- **Day 10**: Implement the client component and tests.
+- **Day 11**: Finalize documentation, end-to-end tests, and prepare for delivery.
+- **Day 12-13**: Buffer day for any unforeseen issues or delays.
+
+# Hardware and Software Requirements
+The host can run on any hardware that supports a Linux operating system with cgroups v2 and `systemd`. This covers most
+modern Linux distributions including Ubuntu, Debian, Fedora, Arch and their derivatives, such as Mint. The reason for
+this is simple. `systemd` provides a simple and reliable way to manage cgroups, which are essential for resource
+management and isolation of jobs. It is completely possible to implement this without `systemd` and manually control
+cgroups, but that would increase the complexity of this project for very little value (such manual management involves
+creating the hierarchy and then manually writing various parameters to files in `/sys/fs/cgroup`, which has permission
+and ownership implications). `systemd` provides `systemd-run` for exactly this type of program, and using it
+addresses a number of edge cases that the requirements call out, such as correctly handling orphaned processes when the
+server crashes or is killed.
+
+*Note*: `systemd` is not required to run the server itself, only to manage the jobs that it spawns. The server can be
+run under any init system or even without one, as long as the host OS supports cgroups v2 and `systemd` is installed.
+
+*Note*: A future improvement would be to add support for non-`systemd` systems by manually managing cgroups, but this is not
+a requirement for this challenge, just that resource limits be enforced. Moving to a non-`systemd` model but using process
+groups and manually writing to cgroups control files, is easy, but not trivial. If the requirement to manage resources
+per job was lifted then this could trivially be portable enough to run on MacOS as well.
